title: The Call Stack and Synchronous Execution
concept: JavaScript is a single-threaded language that manages function execution through the call stack

steps.title: Initialize Log Array
steps.explanation:
Create the `log` array.
We'll use this array to record the order in which functions execute.
steps.keyInsight: The array is stored in the Heap, and the variable holds a reference to that array's address.

steps.title: Call first() — Create Stack Frame
steps.explanation:
When first() is called, a **stack frame** is created and pushed onto the call stack.
This frame holds the function's parameters, local variables, and the **return address**.

**Analogy**: It's like opening a 'first project' folder on your desk.
Other work is paused for now.
steps.keyInsight: Calling a function = creating a stack frame (allocating memory)
steps.analogy: It's like opening a 'first project' folder on your desk. Other work is paused for now.
steps.tip: If too many frames pile up, you get a **Stack Overflow** error.

steps.title: Execute log.push('first start')
steps.explanation:
We've entered the first() function body.
Add 'first start' to the `log` array.
Now log = ['first start'].
steps.keyInsight: Array's push() mutates the original array in place.

steps.title: Call second() — Pushed onto Call Stack
steps.explanation:
While first() is executing, second() gets called.
second() is pushed on top of the call stack.
steps.keyInsight: When a function calls another function, the new function is stacked on top. **The last function called finishes first.**
steps.analogy: Imagine a plate for first() with a plate for second() stacked on top. You have to remove the second() plate before you can access the first() plate.
steps.tip: **LIFO (Last In First Out)**: The last thing in is the first thing out. This is the fundamental principle of a stack.
steps.misconception: Watch out for the parallel execution misconception! second() must completely finish before first() resumes.

steps.title: Execute log.push('second')
steps.explanation:
Inside second(), log.push('second') executes.
Now log = ['first start', 'second'].
steps.keyInsight: Only the function at the top of the call stack executes. The first() below it is 'waiting'.

steps.title: second() Ends — Removed from Call Stack
steps.explanation:
second() has finished and is popped off the call stack.
first() is back on top.
steps.keyInsight: When a function ends, it's removed from the call stack. The function below it then resumes execution.
steps.analogy: We've removed the second() plate, so now we can access the first() plate.
steps.tip: **pop**: removing the top item from a stack. The opposite (adding) is **push**.

steps.title: Return to first() — log.push('first end')
steps.explanation:
second() has finished, so first() resumes from where it **left off**.
log becomes ['first start', 'second', 'first end'].
steps.keyInsight: The call stack remembers where to return after a function call. This is why it's called a 'call stack'.
steps.tip: **Return address**: the call stack also stores 'where to go back to' after each call.

steps.title: first() Ends
steps.explanation:
first() has also reached its end.
first() is removed from the call stack.
The call stack is now empty.
steps.keyInsight: Empty call stack = no function executing = program moves on to the next code

steps.title: log.push('done') — Execute Global Code
steps.explanation:
The first() call has finished, so the next line executes.
log = ['first start', 'second', 'first end', 'done']
steps.keyInsight: Synchronous code runs top to bottom, sequentially. If a function is called, execution waits until that function completely finishes.
steps.analogy: Like a cooking recipe — one step must finish before moving to the next. You can't do multiple steps at the same time.

steps.title: Check the Final Result
steps.explanation:
Print the log array.
It's recorded as ['first start', 'second', 'first end', 'done'].
This order proves the LIFO behavior of the call stack.
steps.keyInsight: 'second' was recorded before 'first end' because second() had to completely finish before first() could resume.

quiz.explanation:
a() executes and adds 1 → b() is called and pushed onto the call stack → 2 is added → b() ends and a() resumes → 3 is added.
JavaScript is single-threaded, so 'simultaneously' is impossible.

misconceptions.wrong: JavaScript can execute multiple functions at the same time
misconceptions.correct:
JavaScript is **single-threaded**.
Only the function at the top of the call stack executes at any given moment.
misconceptions.why:
There is only one main thread in the browser.
What looks like simultaneous execution is made possible by the 'event loop', which you'll learn about in the next lesson.

misconceptions.wrong: Calling a function inside a function runs them in parallel
misconceptions.correct:
No.
It's just a 'nested call' — they still execute one at a time, in order.
misconceptions.why:
The call stack is a **LIFO (Last In First Out)** structure.
The function stacked on top (called last) must finish and be removed from the stack before the function below can continue.

keyTakeaway: Call stack = tracks currently executing functions, single-threaded = one at a time, LIFO = last in first out
